Paragraph 14 places the request qualifier immediately before demonstration; confirmation remains separately stated, while footnote 5 describes confirmation and demonstration together without repeating the qualifier, creating a reading issue that none of the candidates resolves.

Paragraph 14 and footnote 5 require substantive confirmation and demonstration concerning soundness, ownership records and smart-contract integrity, including minimum compliance with paragraphs 10–13 and high confidence concerning vulnerabilities or security flaws; request existence implements none of these standards.

Paragraphs 15 and 16 separately attach requests to third-party audit or verification and satisfactory legal opinion; neither action nor its request can automatically substitute for paragraph 14 demonstration.

Retained responsibility, allocation of operational authority, supervisory conduct and actual operational or record-keeping outcomes are distinct; the supplied section 6.8 permits specified parties to maintain the register, and section 6.11C concerns valuation supervision rather than establishing a universal tokenisation supervision test.

The supplied intermediary provisions concern their specified activities and actors and cannot automatically supply missing Product Provider compliance tests; Part A factors, omitted footnote 2 and the complete paragraphs 10–13 remain unresolved dependencies.
All six candidates declare TRUE_IS_SATISFIED, but none evaluates substantive performance; scope membership establishes applicability, not fulfilment.

node.dfbeb05a271dfdc22f59b8d9, deferred.2249d844381920c4bb3ae2cf and deferred.481ce79be4fc0611266ee787 grant unconditional satisfaction within scope without source support.

Paragraph 14 most directly conditions demonstration on an SFC request; confirmation remains unconditioned, while footnote 5 leaves a supported rival reading of an unqualified demonstration expectation.
Footnote 5 imports paragraphs 10–13, whose complete requirements are unavailable; full compliance cannot be established from the supplied excerpts.
Paragraphs 15 and 16 concern separate requests for third-party audit or verification and a satisfactory legal opinion; a paragraph 14 demonstration request cannot substitute for either.

The remaining excerpts distinguish retained responsibility despite outsourcing, register maintenance, valuation supervision and intermediary due diligence; none establishes that authority allocation, supervisory conduct or a request alone proves operational outcomes or fulfilment.

All six extracted claims are supported by the supplied source, subject to their stated role and activity conditions; paragraph 17's SHOULD classification represents the directive reminder rather than a literal modal verb.

The three request-based candidates make a paragraph 14 demonstration request necessary and sufficient for a TRUE_IS_SATISFIED result, without source support for treating a request as performance or for using that request to trigger the distinct paragraph 15 and 16 duties.
The three constant-true candidates declare satisfaction for every in-scope provider without assessing conduct or outcomes; the source does not authorize that unconditional conclusion.

Paragraph 14 distinguishes confirmation from demonstration upon request, while footnote 5 jointly describes confirmation and demonstration; their possible attachment readings do not justify either unconditional satisfaction or satisfaction from the request alone.

No SFC demonstration request does not establish failure or fulfilment of ongoing responsibilities, confirmation, register maintenance, or applicable intermediary duties, and does not establish whether a separate audit or legal-opinion request exists.

Paragraph 10, footnote 1 and the ownership-record provision distinguish retained provider responsibility from delegated register maintenance and actual operational and record-keeping outcomes; none of the candidates assesses these distinctions.

The additional address-notification requirement in section 6.8 is distinct from register maintenance, and section 6.11C's selection, monitoring and supervision duties concern third-party valuation within their own scope; neither supplies a general satisfaction standard for these candidates.

Footnote 5 references paragraphs 10 to 13, but their full contents and the referenced Appendix factors are not supplied, so complete substantive compliance cannot be established from this packet or from the candidates' externally supplied scope classifications.

node.f189039671da0fc054c157bd, deferred.9d6ef75f1b5f4ae94e41f5d5 and deferred.a2190f7599ca8c478be5d897 equate an SFC demonstration request with satisfaction; paragraph 14 makes the request a trigger for demonstration, not evidence that the provider has fulfilled its duties.

node.dfbeb05a271dfdc22f59b8d9, deferred.2249d844381920c4bb3ae2cf and deferred.481ce79be4fc0611266ee787 return unconditional satisfaction within scope, without source support for dispensing with confirmation, responsibility, operational soundness or ownership records.

Paragraph 14 distinguishes confirmation from demonstration upon request; footnote 5 states their minimum substantive content without repeating the trigger, so any rival reading of that relationship must be preserved rather than resolved through a request-only or constant result.

Absent an SFC request, the demonstration trigger may remain inactive, but this does not establish fulfillment of confirmation or continuing substantive duties; paragraphs 15 and 16 separately condition obtaining third-party audit or verification and a satisfactory legal opinion on SFC requests.
The supplied scope classifications do not implement the circular's complete applicability perimeter, and the public-offering explanation in footnote 1 does not establish that perimeter by itself.

UT Code 6.8 identifies responsibility for maintaining a register and separately requires its address on request; it does not displace Product Provider responsibility, while the valuation-specific supervision provisions in 6.11C cannot automatically supply a tokenisation-wide compliance test.

The intermediary provisions address distinct actors and activities: paragraph 13 preserves responsibility despite outsourcing, and paragraphs 17–18 reference Parts A and B; footnote 1's Product Provider reference imports only applicable Part A considerations.

None of the candidates distinguishes allocation of authority, supervisory conduct and operational or record-keeping outcomes; the supplied text does not establish that any one of these alone proves fulfillment without an applicable standard and actual facts.
All six candidates declare TRUE_IS_SATISFIED but supply no evidence of performance: provider status alone or the existence of a request is unsupported as a sufficient condition for satisfaction.
The three request-based candidates also make a request necessary for a true result, although ownership records, operational compatibility and confirmation are not expressly conditional on a request.

Footnote 5 can be read as elaborating paragraph 14 with its demonstration trigger carried through, or as independently expressing demonstration without that condition; neither reading makes the request itself performance.
No SFC request does not establish fulfillment of underlying duties; under the inherited-trigger reading it leaves demonstration untriggered, while confirmation remains applicable.

Paragraphs 15 and 16 separately condition third-party audit or verification and a satisfactory legal opinion on SFC requests; those requests cannot automatically substitute for the paragraph 14 demonstration request.

Paragraph 10 and footnote 1 preserve ultimate responsibility despite outsourcing; allocation of authority, supervisory conduct and actual operational or record-keeping outcomes remain distinct matters requiring applicable standards and facts.

The register provisions, valuation-specific supervision provision and intermediary provisions do not establish performance of these Product Provider duties or justify importing their distinct actors and modal strengths without an applicability analysis.
